---
name: work-planner
description: >-
  Plans and maintains agent-engineering work on GitHub: proposals, initiatives, epics, tasks and theme boards. Use to propose work or scope a problem; plan or break down work; raise, restructure, align or renumber an initiative or epic; check issue format, criteria, dependencies or delivery; fold review findings into issues; sync completed work and close what is finished; advance a board, decide what moves to ready or what to pick up next; deliver board work or dispatch ready tasks; understand or explain a pull request, write its architecture overview or diagram its changes; hoist, triage or find a home for orphan issues; produce a standup or Slack status update; or revise the work-planner skill itself.
---

# Work Planner

Work Planner plans work as GitHub issues and keeps the plan current until the work is delivered. The issues are the plan:

- **Proposal**  States the problem and the goal, with no Work Breakdown.
- **Initiative**  States a goal and lists its epics.
- **Epic**  Lists its tasks in a Work Breakdown table.
- **Task**  One pull request's worth of work.
- **Standalone issue**  Work outside any initiative.
- **[Hot-fix](artifacts/hotfix-body.md)**  A fix to a long-lived branch beside all queued work.

Each theme's project board shows where its items stand. The [proposals board](configuration.md#proposals-board) holds proposals. A planning record holds what an initiative leaves out: the evidence, the decisions and each review.

Read [Rules](rules.md) and [Conventions](conventions.md) before selecting a mode.

## Modes

Select the mode as appropriate to fulfill the user request:

- **[Propose](modes/propose-mode.md)**
  - Forward-looking, scoped to one problem
  - Scoping a problem nothing is planned against yet
  - Raising a proposal issue with optional board placement
- **[Plan](modes/plan-mode.md)**
  - Forward-looking, scoped to one approved proposal
  - Turning an approved proposal into initiatives
  - Raising, breaking down and restructuring initiatives and epics
  - Review passes of a plan against its goal, dependencies included
  - Renumbering of epics and tasks
  - Folding review findings into issues
- **[Align](modes/align-mode.md)**
  - Backward-looking, scoped to one epic, initiative or board
  - Checks of existing issues against their templates and the rules that bind them, with fixes
  - Acceptance criteria checked for verifiability and against the sources the initiative marks
  - Epic branch structure and task pull request bases brought to the delivery shape
- **[Sync](modes/sync-mode.md)**
  - Backward-looking, scoped to one epic, initiative or board
  - Delivery recorded against the issues that planned it
  - Closure of complete task issues, epics and initiatives
  - The theme board brought current with its issues
- **[Advance](modes/advance-mode.md)**
  - Forward-looking, scoped to one board
  - Placement of initiatives and epics as In Progress or as Ready, and of hot-fixes as their [Board Status](artifacts/hotfix.md#board-status) gives
  - A parallel work map for initiatives with no priority
- **[Deliver](modes/deliver-mode.md)**
  - Forward-looking, scoped to one board
  - Delivery of a theme board's work, each unit planned, implemented and raised as a pull request
  - Dispatch of one session per unit of work
  - Merging task pull requests through the shared delivery procedure
- **[Understand](modes/understand-mode.md)**
  - Backward-looking, scoped to one pull request
  - An architecture overview of one pull request
  - Structural and functional diagrams of its changes
  - The order to read the diff in
- **[Hoist](modes/hoist-mode.md)**
  - Forward-looking, scoped to a repository's orphan issues
  - Discovery of orphan issues
  - Placements for each in an existing or new initiative, epic or task, or as a hot-fix
- **[Standup](modes/standup-mode.md)**
  - Backward-looking, scoped to one board's reporting window
  - Standup summaries of a theme's board for a Slack channel
- **[Revise](modes/revise-mode.md)**
  - Forward-looking, scoped to this skill's own files
  - Changes to SKILL.md, its modes, artifacts, references and scripts

## Dependencies

- **GitHub CLI (`gh`).**
- **Sandbox.** (`scripts/sbx`).
- **Python 3.10 or later.**
- **git.**
- **GitNexus.**
- **Sub-agents.**
- **Epic-base merge permission.**
  The agent harness grants the [Merge Permission](artifacts/pull-request.md#merge-permission) Deliver needs.

# Rules

- **Linked sections.**
  Read a heading-linked section and its subsections, stopping before the next heading of equal or higher level. Read that file's Prerequisites first; reading prerequisites does not execute procedures. A mode named in another mode's Prerequisites is read as a document, and its own Prerequisites load only where a step runs it. Preserve boundaries in batched reads and recover truncated output. Reuse complete prerequisites already read at the same revision. Explicit whole-document requirements still apply.
- **Decisions.**
  Ask one at a time, following the [interview rules](guidelines.md#modes). A decision the run's [allowance](artifacts/plan-change.md#allowance) covers is taken with its recommended option rather than asked. Record each decision in the affected issues and, when there is one, the planning record.
- **Layers.**
  Modes, protocols, artifacts. A mode aggregates protocol calls, as an application calls services; a protocol runs artifact operations and other protocols; an artifact runs neither. A call goes down the stack, never up. A mode reaches an artifact operation directly only where no protocol owns that change.
- **Execution.**
  A call passes its named inputs. A protocol is one change that lands in several artifacts together, and is run whole. Run another mode, a protocol, or a named subsection only where the procedure calls it; finish that call and return its result before continuing, unless the procedure explicitly dispatches concurrent work.

# Conventions

- **Session.**
  Once per session, before the first `gh` call, unset `GH_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_TOKEN` so `gh` uses its keyring login. Where shell state does not persist between commands, confirm instead that neither is set in the shell profile.
- **Repository.**
  `gh` resolves `{owner}/{repo}` from the git remote of the directory it runs in, so run `gh` commands inside a checkout of the repository that holds the issues. `{other}` is a further repository the board's issues live in.
- **Checkouts.**
  A command that runs git or GitNexus where it stands declares `**Acts on:** the checkout it runs in.`, and each call to it, or to an operation running it, names one as `the <name> checkout`. Each mode and protocol declares `**Runs in:** the <name> checkout.`, as does a procedure subsection running elsewhere.
  - `project`  The repository's main working tree.
  - `epic base`  An epic base's worktree.
  - `unit`  A unit's task worktree.
  - `engineering`  The [engineering branch](configuration.md#planning-records)'s worktree.
  - `review`  A pull request's detached review worktree.
- **Bodies.**
  - Bodies and long comments always go through a file (`-F body=@file`), never inline, which avoids quoting.
  - **Example.**  workflow-server's dynamic-shell restrictions deny a body inlined in the command.
  - A plan's draft bodies are files of its [planning record](artifacts/planning-record.md#layout). Keep every other body file in a working directory outside the repository.
- **Scripts.**
  Scripts run under `sbx`, invoked by its absolute path from `<workspace>`, the checkout holding this skill. A script that reaches the tracker calls `gh` itself, and one that adds a worktree writes the repository's git directory, which `sbx` leaves read-only; each runs from `<workspace>` outside `sbx`.
- **Boards.**
  A project board sits under `users/{owner}`, or `orgs/{owner}` when `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo} --jq .owner.type` is `Organization`.
- **Example values.**  Substitute the real ones:
  - `936` an initiative issue, `943` and `937` its epics, `637` a task issue, `874` an orphan, `946` an initiative off the board, `960` a proposal;
  - `950` a pull request, `I07` and `I08` initiative numbers;
  - board `9`, workflow-server's Canon theme, and `419167630` its Status field id;
  - `1` the Initiative Template board, `13` a board copied from it;
  - `14` the Proposals Template, `15` the Proposals board;
  - `m2ux` the user.
  - `<checkout>` any checkout of the project, a linked worktree included.

# Revise Mode

Changes the skill itself: SKILL.md, its modes, artifacts, references and scripts.

**Runs in:** the project checkout.

## Prerequisites

Read these files first.

- [Skill Guidelines](../../guidelines.md)
- [Guidelines](../guidelines.md)

## Procedure

The main path meets [Outcomes](#outcomes).

1. **Read the guidelines.**
   Read the [shared skill guidelines](../../guidelines.md) and [skill guidelines](../guidelines.md) whole before the first edit.
2. **Understand the request.**
   Interview the user, as an [Interview](../guidelines.md#modes), until the change and its scope are clear.
   - Find every file the change touches: the rule's home, each file that cites it, and any script, docstring or test that states it.
3. **Work in a worktree.**
   Branch a worktree for the change.
   - Commit each distinct change as its own commit.
4. **Revise.**
   Make the change in the rule's one home.
   - Link to it from every other file that needs it.
   - Write it to the guidelines' layout, prose, link and command rules as it is written, not in a later pass.
   - When the user states a new writing rule, add it to the applicable shared or skill-specific guidelines before validation and delivery.
5. **Check against the guidelines.**
   Read every changed file against the [shared skill guidelines](../../guidelines.md) and [skill guidelines](../guidelines.md), checking:
   - The description, when the skill's reach changed.
   - One line per item, bold leads on their own line, and sub-bullets for discrete points.
   - Each rule stated once, and no description of replaced behaviour left anywhere.
   - Every command linked to its operation section.
   - Every link and anchor resolving.
   - [Progressive disclosure](../../guidelines.md#progressive-disclosure), including complete common sections and caller prerequisites.
   - Fix each departure.
6. **Verify.**
   - Run [Run Tests](#run-tests) when an executable script, its consumed template or a test changed.
   - When SKILL.md changes, confirm its frontmatter opens and closes with `---` and holds `name` and `description`.
   - Run [Check Skill Files](#check-skill-files) for every affected skill.
   - Run [Compare Section Bodies](#compare-section-bodies) when the change moves a section between files, and read each section it reports as added, removed or differing.
   - Apply [disclosure verification](../../guidelines.md#disclosure-verification) with the skill's [representative scenarios](../guidelines.md#progressive-disclosure).
   - Resolve every required file, command and heading without an implicit external dependency.
7. **Deliver.**
   - Commit.
   - Push.
   - Report what changed in each file.

## Outcomes

- **The skill matches the request.**
  The user has the change they asked for in the skill, committed and pushed.
- **The guidelines hold.**
  The change agrees with the guidelines, and a new rule the user stated for how the skill is written is part of that change.

## Operations

### Run Tests

Runs the skill's script tests.

**Inputs:** Workspace checkout containing the installed skill and its tests.

```bash
cd "<workspace>/skills/work-planner" && "<workspace>/scripts/sbx" python3 -m unittest discover -s test
```

### Check Skill Files

Checks the affected skill's files against the rules the shared skill guidelines state.

**Inputs:** Workspace checkout and affected skill directory; repeat the skill argument for additional affected skills.

```bash
cd "<workspace>" && "<workspace>/scripts/sbx" python3 skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py "<skill-directory>"
```

**Example:** Work Planner in the selected checkout.

```bash
cd "<workspace>" && "<workspace>/scripts/sbx" python3 skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py skills/work-planner
```

### Compare Section Bodies

Compares every third-level section's body between the change's base and its head, so a section damaged in a move is reported.

**Inputs:** Workspace checkout, the base and head revisions, and each skill directory the move touches.

- A relative link target is compared by its fragment alone, so a retargeted link is no difference.
- Each section is reported as identical, moved, added, removed or differing, with a diff of each differing body and the section count at each revision.
- Exit 1 means a section was added, removed or differs.

```bash
cd "<workspace>" && "<workspace>/scripts/sbx" python3 skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py --compare "<base>" "<head>" "<skill-directory>"
```

# Skill Guidelines

How a skill's own files are written: SKILL.md, the references, the templates, and the scripts' docstrings. Every change to a skill follows them. A skill with rules of its own keeps them in `guidelines.md` beside its entry point or in `references/guidelines.md`, and those rules define the structure of every directory it adds.

## Frontmatter

- **Fields.**
  - `name` and `description`, and `hooks` when the skill declares a hook. No other field.
  - `name` is kebab-case and matches the skill's folder.
- **Hooks.**
  - A skill declares a hook when a check it owns must run at every tool call that could break it, not only at a step its procedure names.
  - The hook's command runs a script in the skill's own scripts folder, which exits at once on a call outside its check.
  - Claude Code registers the hook when the skill is invoked and runs it for the rest of the session. Cursor ignores the field.
- **Description.**
  - It states what the skill covers and the requests that call for it, as the phrases a user would say: "plan the work", "audit workflow X".
  - It carries at least one such phrase for each mode, naming the mode by its own word in any form: "audit workflow X" reaches Audit, "revising this skill" reaches Revise. The description alone decides whether the skill loads.
  - It carries no procedure; what each mode does is in the body.
  - It stays under the 1,024-character skill limit.

## Files

- **SKILL.md.**  The skill's entry point, at the top of its folder.
- **References.**
  - A mode file is named `<mode>-mode.md`. `references/` holds `guidelines.md` when the skill has rules of its own, and each guide the modes share.
  - A skill may add directories of its own, one for its modes among them, and keep its guidelines beside SKILL.md. Its guidelines state what those files carry and the sections they take, and `structure.json` beside SKILL.md declares those sections to the shared check.
  - Scripts and tests each have a folder of their own. Standalone templates use `templates/`.
- **Shared.**
  `skills/` holds this file beside the `scripts/` and `test/` folders for checks that every skill runs. A check binding one skill lives in that skill's own folders.

## SKILL.md structure

- **Top-level sections.**
  - Modes, Rules, Conventions and Dependencies, in that order, each optional.
  - The Opening stands under the title, ahead of them. Anything else the entry point needs is a sub-section under one of them.
- **Opening.**
  One sentence on what the skill does, then a bulleted list with one item for each thing it acts on.
- **Modes.**
  - Each mode is its bold name, without the word "mode", linking to its reference file.
  - Beneath it, a bulleted list that selects the mode, since the reader holds a request and picks one mode from this list alone:
    - The first item states the mode's direction and what it is scoped to, and nothing else: `Backward-looking, scoped to one initiative`.
    - Each further item is one line: a noun phrase or a gerund phrase naming a request this mode answers.
    - An item earns its place only where a request reaches this mode because of it. At most five follow the first.
    - A step the mode takes once selected stays in the mode file, as does a distinction from another mode.
    - A mode the mode runs for itself goes unnamed, since naming it routes that mode's own requests here.
    - It has no trailing full stop, no purpose clause, and no board status outside that phrase.
- **Rules.**
  A statement that binds every mode goes in Rules, never as loose prose in another section.
- **Conventions.**
  The skill-wide prerequisites that [Conventions](#commands) places in the entry point.
- **Dependencies.**
  Every tool, sandbox, runtime, branch and harness capability the skill relies on is named in Dependencies, with what it is needed for.
- **Commands.**
  SKILL.md holds no command of its own, so it takes no Commands section.

## Procedure files

- **What the file carries selects the set.**
  - A procedure is a top-level section carrying a numbered step, whatever its heading names it, as [Commands](#commands) defines it.
  - A file carrying one takes the sections below. A catalog, a context file and a contract file state what a procedure consults, and nothing about them is a sequence, so each keeps its own shape.
  - A skill's entry point takes [its own structure](#skillmd-structure) whatever it carries.
- **Top-level sections.**
  - Prerequisites, Procedure, Reference, Rules and Commands, in that order, each optional but for Procedure.
  - Anything else the file needs is a sub-section under one of them, so a diverse title names a part of a known whole.
- **What the reader does with a heading places it.**
  - Reference holds what a step consults or produces: a table, an output shape, a vocabulary.
  - Rules holds what binds the file whatever step it is on.
  - An alternative way in is a step of the Procedure.
- **Procedure.**
  A `## Procedure` of numbered steps, each opening with a bold label. Where the file holds several procedures, each is a sub-section of it.

## Layout

- **One line per item.**
  Each paragraph and list item is one line. No file is hard-wrapped at a column; the editor wraps.
- **Bold leads.**
  - A bold lead is a label. When the label and its body fit on one line of at most 100 characters, indent included, the body stays on it, two spaces after the label: `- **Epic**  Lists its tasks in a Work Breakdown table.`
  - A longer body goes on the next line, indented under the bullet.
  - A label that is a phrase ends in a full stop. A bare name, such as a mode or an issue type, takes none.
  - No bold words open a running sentence. A step such as "**Fetch** each issue" becomes the label "**Fetch.**" with "Fetch each issue …" beneath it.
- **Sub-bullets.**
  An item that describes several discrete points lists them as sub-bullets. A single sentence, or a simple list within one sentence, stays as it is.
- **Heading spacing.**
  A blank line stands above every heading, except one opening the file or its body after the frontmatter, so no list item or paragraph reads it in.
- **Bounded prose.**
  A run of prose under one heading, its paragraphs counted together, is at most eight lines. Longer prose splits into named sub-sections, leaving the linked heading where it is. A list or table is one structure and is not split to meet this.

## Prose

- **Succinct.**  Plain words, and no sentence that another already carries.
- **One home per rule.**
  - Each rule is stated once: in SKILL.md, the mode that owns it, or the guide the modes share.
  - Every other file cites it by link, never restates it. A caller passes inputs and routes results without repeating the linked operation’s description, output fields or guarantees.
  - A skill's guide states no rule under the label and section title of a rule in this file.
- **Deciding operation.**
  - Each labelled rule a guide states names the operations that decide it, in `rules.json` beside that guide, keyed `<section-anchor>/<label-anchor>`.
  - An operation is a kind of finding the shared check reports, or `review`, the read of a change against the guidelines that a skill's Revise procedure runs.
- **The design as it is.**
  Present tense, with no account of what the text replaced: no "previously", "no longer" or "instead of".
- **Terms.**
  - One concept carries one term. After a rename, every use of the old term goes, in prose, docstrings and identifiers.
  - `vocabulary.json` beside SKILL.md maps each concept's term to the terms it retires. A retired term stands nowhere in the skill's markdown outside code, nor anywhere in its scripts.
- **One mood for parallel sections.**
  Sibling sections whose titles end in one word, such as Main Coverage and Docker Coverage, state one kind of thing, so each opens in the same mood: each says what holds, or each directs the reader. A dependency between the commands a section names is stated as one, and a section that directs an order of work is a procedure.

## Links

- **Files.**
  A reference to another markdown file in the skill is a relative link, never a code span.
- **Link text.**
  The link sits on the noun that names the thing: the mode, the guide, the command, the template.
- **Selection links.**
  A link naming the next operation, section or route points wherever that content sits, forward included. The reader chooses from it rather than needing to hold it already.
- **Prerequisite citation.**
  A citation asserting the reader must already hold a section earns its place only where that section is in another file, opened for its own reason. Name it: `Read [Audit Command Conventions](change-surface.md#audit-command-conventions) first.`
  - Within one file, position carries the requirement and the citation is dropped: conventions sit ahead of the procedures and commands they govern.
  - A prerequisite citation pointing further down its own file is a defect, whatever its wording. A sequential reader meets it after the point it was meant to serve.
- **Resolution.**
  Every link resolves to a file that exists, and every anchor to one heading in it: no two headings of a file share an anchor.

## Commands

- **One spec per operation.**
  - Every command has a sub-section named for what it does: Fetch issue, Run guard suite.
  - A script used several ways has a spec for each use.
- **Local to the procedure.**
  - A specification sits in the file whose procedure runs it, in a `## Commands` section at the end of that file.
  - A single catalog holds only those specifications most of whose entries have several callers. Where a block of a catalog has one caller, it belongs to that caller.
  - A caller is a procedure that runs the command. A sibling specification, and any passage of prose naming a command, does not make the file holding it a caller.
  - Reach is what a reader must load: a step's citation, a specification's citation, and a prerequisite. A specification citing another command reaches it without calling it, so reach measures retrieval and leaves placement to callers.
  - Placement follows the skill's declared structure. A structure whose commands belong to their subject keeps each there, however few procedures call it.
  - A specification no procedure runs has no caller to place it, so it stays with the subject of the file whose prose or sibling specification names it. One nothing cites has no reader, whatever structure holds it.
  - A procedure is a section carrying numbered steps, whatever its heading names it. The step is the author stating that the reader performs these, in this order, and is the only place a file records that.
  - Prose runs nothing whatever its mood, order or count: a sentence routing three commands in sequence names them as a statement of what one command does names it. State a route as steps to call them.
  - SKILL.md holds no specification. A command the entry point names is specified in the file whose procedure runs it, or in the catalog.
  - A specification with two owners has one home and a link from the other. A count of those links that keeps growing says the split is in the wrong place.
- **Spec layout.**
  - Each spec opens with a one-line, succinct description of what the command does.
  - Detail a caller needs, such as flags, inputs or refusals, follows as bullets, then the command block.
- **Named by link.**
  - Prose names a spec by linking to its sub-section, mid-sentence: "run [Check Body Format](work-planner/artifacts/issue-body.md#check-body-format) on each epic".
  - A command body is inlined only in the file that owns the spec.
  - A mode file holds a shell or unlabelled code block only inside its command specifications.
- **Interface.**
  - A command reaches GitHub through REST wherever REST supports the operation, and through current GraphQL where it does not.
  - A specification whose command sends GraphQL, itself or through a script it runs, states what REST lacks on a `**REST gap:**` line.
  - Projects (classic) fields, types, mutations and REST endpoints are never used. Project operations use Projects V2.
- **Conventions.**
  - Session setup, execution location, example values and other skill-wide prerequisites stand where a procedure reaching them opens no further file: SKILL.md, which selects the mode, or the file holding the operations those procedures open anyway.
  - Conventions governing one procedure's commands sit in that procedure's file, ahead of its Commands section.

## Progressive Disclosure

- **Placement.**
  Keep shared purpose, mode selection and essential constraints in the entry point. Link conditional detail where the active mode needs it.
- **Applicability.**
  State the condition beside a conditional link and require the reader to resolve it before loading the instructions. Select checks before retrieving their command specs.
- **Reading boundaries.**
  Link the smallest complete section the caller needs. The skill's reading rules define a heading link as that section and its subsections, stopping before the next heading of equal or higher level. Whole-file links identify required complete documents.
- **File size.**
  A heading link names a section; a reader takes the file. Size each file to one role's whole context, and split a file that carries guidance that role never uses. A boundary the reader need not honour is not a budget.
- **Prerequisites.**
  Provide the context needed to use each section in the file that holds it. Link it only where the reader would not otherwise reach it, as a [prerequisite citation](#links). Split files when section routing still brings unrelated guidance into context.
- **Common context.**
  Group prerequisites shared by all specific sections into one named common section, with any common subsections nested beneath it. Specific sections sit outside that heading's boundary. Keep prerequisites used by only some sections with those sections or in a separately linked section.
- **Caller routing.**
  A calling document links the common section once on a required path before its first specific section, then links specific sections at their points of use. Every supported entry path reaches that prerequisite link; an unlinked preamble or sibling section supplies no context. Reuse complete prerequisite content already read at the same revision.
- **Prohibition and structure.**
  A rule telling a reader to retrieve less says the file carries more than that reader needs. Remove the surplus rather than policing the read.
- **Batched reads.**
  Preserve each link's boundary when batching retrieval. Batch selected whole files or separate section ranges; each range excludes unrelated intervening content. Inspect headings to locate boundaries.
- **Complete output.**
  Bound reads and output volume so required content is returned completely. Retrieve missing sections when output is truncated; a request for content is not evidence of receipt.

## Disclosure Verification

- **Required context.**
  Every revision traces a representative request through each affected mode's required reads, including prerequisites, subsections and explicit whole-file requirements. Check every supported entry path for common context before specific sections, reuse across multiple operations and exclusion of unrelated sections. Necessity follows the task and affected consumers; another mode's guidance can be required.
- **Live checks.**
  When a revision changes reading paths, test representative requests with independent sub-agents in fresh contexts. Give them the skill, realistic tasks, necessary inputs and authority limits, without expected reading choices or prior findings. Repeat affected scenarios before claiming consistent behavior. Record unavailable live validation as an evidence gap.
- **Observed behavior.**
  Inspect actual tool calls, returned content and task results. Missing necessary context or loading unrelated content fails the disclosure check. Report structural validation and live behavior separately, preserving observed failures.
- **Performance.**
  Record unnecessary content, repeated reads, truncation and task correctness. Claims of context-token savings require a comparable baseline with the same tasks, inputs and execution conditions; file or word counts establish only their stated measurements.
- **What a walk can settle.**
  Measure the volume a walk retrieves, which its transcript settles outright. Retrieval order measures file layout wherever the reader loads the file whole, so it can show a citation failing and never show one working. A test of citation efficacy needs a target that broad reading does not already reach.

## Changes

- **Worktrees.**
  Make skill changes in a dedicated linked worktree on the change's branch. Preserve existing edits in the project-root checkout. Corrections to an open pull request stay on its branch.
- **Current preferences.**
  Keep the guidelines aligned with the user's explicit, non-reverted preferences. A later correction supersedes the earlier preference; update its existing rule in the same change. Shared rules belong here and skill-specific rules belong in that skill's guidelines.
- **Everything that names it.**
  A rename or a move updates every reference: folder, `name`, heading, script paths, links and anchors.
- **Stale claims.**
  After a behaviour change, search the skill for any description of the old behaviour and restate it.
- **Verified.**
  The skill's tests and affected shared-checker or integration suites pass, `skills/scripts/check_skill_files.py` reports no finding for every skill the change touches, and [disclosure verification](#disclosure-verification) is recorded before the change is committed. State which checks ran and distinguish local evidence from external workflow execution.

# Guidelines

The rules this skill's files follow alongside the [shared skill guidelines](../guidelines.md). Modes, protocols and artifacts use the directory-specific structures below. A rule that binds only modes, only protocols, only artifacts, or only references is in that section.

## Titles

- **Title case.**
  A heading, a board title, an issue or pull request name and subtitle, and a template section heading are in title case.
  - A short word stays lowercase unless it is first or last: a, an, the, and, but, or, nor, for, as, at, by, in, of, on, to, up, with.
  - Each part of a hyphenated word is capitalized.

  What a protocol changes, and what a blocker leaves unchanged, is stated by the step that changes it. A protocol carries no section restating the result; a reader following the procedure and its links has it already, and a summary goes stale against the steps it describes.
- **Prerequisites.**
  Prerequisites open with `Read these files first.` They list every file the protocol's Procedure links to, including each protocol it runs.
- **No spare parts.**
  A protocol nothing runs is not a protocol. One exists because a mode or another protocol follows it.
- **A new protocol.**
  A new protocol is a new file. An artifact is not edited to name it.
- **Step rules.**
  A rule that binds one step sits in that step. A rule that binds every protocol is added to this section.
- **Sections.**
  Prerequisites, Procedure, then Guidance when the file has an assistive statement that is not a step. Procedure is required. A protocol has no Outcomes, Fields, Rules, Operations or Commands section.

## Artifacts

Read this before adding or changing an artifact.

- **One shape.**
  An artifact owns one subject’s state, invariants and operations. Its shape and the transformations that produce it share that home, with shared executable operations in a subject module. It changes when that subject changes. Locate a procedure by the object and state it produces. A caller or a shared command does not determine ownership.
- **Virtual artifacts.**
  A derived artifact owns its output shape even when it has no persisted document. Fields defines that shape; its operations consume supplied evidence.
- **Descriptions.**
  Describe the artifact's subject and contents directly. Omit inconsequential implementation qualifiers such as virtual. Distinguish proposed changes from applied state where the caller needs that distinction; a queue is not itself proposed merely because its changes await application.
- **Prose API.**
  Artifact operations form a prose-based API addressed by subsection titles. Each names its inputs, the artifact state it reads or changes, and the output it returns. Modes call operation headings; operations call command headings. Related artifacts are supplied as evidence rather than managed through the operation.
- **Operation inputs.**
  Callers address an artifact operation through descriptive input names, such as board fields. CLI flags such as `--fields` belong to the artifact's implementation details, not the calling mode procedure. Repeated calls identify the inputs they refresh and retain.
- **Operation scope.**
  An operation exists because a procedure calls it. Classify the work by its subject and behaviour, not its verb or script name: a read that sequences access steps is an operation, and a plan that derives an artifact's state is an operation.
  - Reading, inspecting, planning, populating and validating are shapes an operation can take, not a set an artifact fills. A sibling operation is no reason to add its counterpart, and a wrapper whose body is one call to another operation is that operation.
- **Bodies and lifecycle.**
  A body artifact populates and validates document content. A subject artifact owns its readiness and completion checks from supplied evidence. Reading evidence about related artifacts does not make a check orchestration; coordinating changes to those artifacts does. Creation, metadata, linking and closure belong to the artifact for the tracked object.
- **No mode, no protocol.**
  An artifact never links to a mode or a protocol, including by naming one in prose.
- **Fields.**
  Fields defines the artifact's shape and the conditions on its elements. Common field conditions hold for the family; a kind supplements them. Fields is a `##` section, with each named field or group under `###`. The kind's template is a subsection of Fields and holds that kind's table. Field conditions do not state user goals. A condition that gates an action sits in the procedure step that performs it.
- **No procedure in Fields.**
  A field condition does not name a procedure, a step, or a command, and it does not link to one.
- **Name.**
  A file that populates a body is named `<subject>-body.md`. Its scope is that population. `issue-body.md` is the shared issue body. A kind file is `proposal-body.md`, `initiative-issue-body.md`, `epic-issue-body.md`, `task-body.md`, `standalone-body.md`, or `hotfix-body.md`.
- **Subject names.**
  Name an artifact for its subject and an operation for its action: `board-queue.md` owns Board Queue, and Plan Board Queue is its operation. A computation script can take the subject name, such as `board-queue.py`.
- **Common file.**
  The common file names no kind. A kind's table, its title, and a check that applies only to that kind live on that kind's file. The common file holds the rules every body shares.
- **Operations.**
  Every procedural sequence occupies a named `###` subsection under Operations, including a kind's population path. Operations itself contains no steps; incorporate any overarching sequence into the named operations that perform its constituent work. Omit Operations when the artifact has only command specifications. Each subsection opens with one line on what it is for, followed by its **Inputs:** line and instructions. The opening line does not restate the steps. A step links to the shape it produces and does not restate it. A kind step links to the common procedure unit it uses and adds only the further population. It does not copy the shared rules.
- **Prerequisites.**
  Prerequisites open with `Read these files first.` They list every file the artifact's Operations, Fields or Commands link to. A kind lists `issue-body.md` because it links to it. The common file does not link to a kind.
- **Operation steps.**
  Address instructions directly to the agent, leading each step with its action. Steps have no separate bold introductory label. Multiple steps use consecutive numbering; an operation with one step uses one bullet and counts as a procedure.
- **Returned output.**
  State what the operation returns within its instructions. Do not add a separate Result line.
- **Population conditions.**
  A population step leads with the writing action and its template or owning operation. Mandatory field conditions follow as nested bullets under that step, linked to their local or shared definitions. Each condition states what must hold; field rules remain at their linked home.
- **Command implementation.**
  Commands holds the artifact's command and access specifications. Operations holds the sequences that call them. Both expose named subsections to callers.
- **No spare parts.**
  An artifact does not carry an operation, a field or a command nothing reaches. An operation no procedure cites is surface that drifts from whatever it wraps, and its capability is already reachable through the operation it would call.
- **A new kind.**
  A new kind is a new file. The common file is not edited to name it.
- **Detail.**
  A change keeps every existing condition. A shorter file is not a reason to drop one.
- **Step rules.**
  Put each action's preconditions and refusal conditions in its governing procedure step. Shared preconditions belong to a common procedure that callers invoke. Command specifications require the resulting evidence or authorization as inputs. A rule that binds every artifact is added to this section.
- **Sections.**
  Prerequisites, Operations, Fields, then Guidance when it has an assistive statement that is not a step or a field condition, then Commands when the file has command specifications. Fields is required. An artifact has no Procedure, Outcomes or Rules section.

## References

Read this before adding or changing a reference.

- **Support.**
  A reference is an ad hoc document that supports the process. It is neither a mode nor an artifact.
- **Shape.**
  It follows the shared sections above. It does not use Prerequisites, Procedure, Fields, Operations, Commands, and Outcomes.
- **Cited only.**
  A reference is only ever referred to. It cites neither a mode nor an artifact.
- **Names.**
  A sentence that names a mode or an artifact loses that name. The statement it made stays.
- **Rules.**
  A rule that binds every reference is added to this section.

## Entry Point

- **Opening.**  The bulleted list has one item for each issue type.
- **Section order.**  The opening, Modes and Dependencies occupy the entry point.
- **Issue bodies.**
  The skill's prose layout applies to its instructions. Issue bodies follow [Issue Body](artifacts/issue-body.md#fields); pull request bodies follow [Pull Request Body](artifacts/pull-request-body.md#fields).
- **Common conventions.**
  The entry point requires [Rules](rules.md) and [Conventions](conventions.md) before mode selection. [Configuration](configuration.md) holds deployed values, reached by their consuming sections. Graph-specific setup belongs to [Repository Graph](artifacts/repository-graph.md).

## Progressive Disclosure

Apply the shared [progressive disclosure](../guidelines.md#progressive-disclosure) and [disclosure verification](../guidelines.md#disclosure-verification) rules to affected callers. Modes are read whole; supporting section reads inherit the mode's command prerequisites.

- **Mode routes.**
  Trace each affected mode through its common conventions, selected operations and supporting guides. Include cross-mode calls and explicit whole-file requirements.
- **Board operations.**
  Exercise a Standup request with captured board inputs, selecting multiple operations and reusing conventions. Preserve the generator's format and unresolved evidence.
- **Graph operations.**
  Exercise an Understand request with a named pull request, verifying graph-specific setup before selected graph commands and exclusion of unrelated command bodies.
- **Revision.**
  Exercise a bounded skill edit with its consumer guidance, required whole-file guidelines, local checks and reused common prerequisites.

## Changes

Follow the shared [change rules](../guidelines.md#changes) for worktree isolation, current user preferences and validation.

- **Planning adoption.**
  Commit and push the reviewed planning folder before applying its design to the installed skill. Keep the planning and installed guidelines aligned with the current preference set.
- **Integrated implementation.**
  Map the complete live skill to its intended homes. Apply document moves, embedded templates, consuming readers, script names, callers and tests together; preserve the existing conditions and remove obsolete paths.
- **Delivery.**
  Run the associated tests and integration checks before opening or updating the implementation pull request. Commit and push the changes from their owning worktrees; subsequent corrections update the same pull request.

# Standup Mode

Summarises a project board as a standup, in Slack markup for pasting into a channel: a paragraph for management on what the window accomplished, then what completed, what is in progress, and what is next. The board's Status is the source, so the summary is as current as the board.

**Runs in:** the project checkout.

## Prerequisites

Read these files first.

- [Board](../artifacts/board.md)
- [Sync Mode](sync-mode.md)
- [Pull Request](../artifacts/pull-request.md)
- [Standup Report](../artifacts/standup-report.md)
- [Issue](../artifacts/issue.md)
- [Epic Issue Body](../artifacts/epic-issue-body.md)
- [Issue Body](../artifacts/issue-body.md)

## Procedure

The main path meets [Outcomes](#outcomes).

1. **Select the scope.**
   Run [Select Project Board](../artifacts/board.md#select-project-board) for the requested board, each requested board when the scope is all, or the theme board of the named initiative.
   - Retain the selected window and initiative filter.
   - Complete steps 2–6 separately for each selected board.
2. **Bring delivery current.**
   - Use the delivery results and board state a caller passed in, where this run follows one that already brought the board current. A request made directly by the user supplies none, so the checkpoint is absent.
   - If the checkpoint is absent:
     - Read the board through [Read Board State](../artifacts/board.md#read-board-state).
     - Treat each selected initiative's delivery state as needing refresh.
   - For initiatives with known delivery changes or unknown freshness, run [Sync Mode](sync-mode.md) for the affected initiatives on that board.
   - Resume the fetch step after their delivery results are saved.
   - Report a blocker that prevents a current summary.
   - Retain it as a gap if presenting a partial report.
3. **Fetch.**
   Run [Read Board State](../artifacts/board.md#read-board-state) with the selected board identity.
   - Run [Fetch All Delivery Pull Requests](../artifacts/pull-request.md#fetch-all-delivery-pull-requests) for the [repositories](../artifacts/board.md#repositories) and items Read Board State returned.
   - Run [Fetch Pull Request Issue Links](../artifacts/pull-request.md#fetch-pull-request-issue-links) for those records.
   - Pass the returned snapshots to Compose Standup Report.
4. **Compose.**
   Call [Compose Standup Report](../artifacts/standup-report.md#compose-standup-report) with the board items, initiative pull request records, complete issue-link snapshot, selected window and initiative filter, resolved off-board initiative records and output paths.
5. **Resolve evidence.**
   For each unresolved initiative:
   - Call [Locate Initiative Issue](../artifacts/issue.md#locate-initiative-issue).
   - Run [Read Tracker Issue](../artifacts/issue.md#read-tracker-issue) for its current JSON.
   - Repeat [Compose Standup Report](../artifacts/standup-report.md#compose-standup-report) with all resolved initiative records, retaining the board items, pull requests, links, selected window and filter. An unavailable record remains a reported gap.
6. **Report.**
   Present the returned report verbatim in a fenced block for copying.
   - Put unresolved findings beneath it.
   - For an epic [Compose Standup Report](../artifacts/standup-report.md#compose-standup-report) returns with an unreadable Work Breakdown:
     - Run [Repair Issue Format](../artifacts/issue-body.md#repair-issue-format) with the epic identity, current JSON, [epic template and field conditions](../artifacts/epic-issue-body.md#fields), required related evidence and output body path.
     - If it confirms a saved correction, repeat steps 3–6 with refreshed records, retaining the selected board, window and initiative filter.
     - If it reports a blocker or no correction, return the unresolved finding without repeating the same repair.

## Outcomes

- **A standup for the window.**
  The user has a summary they can paste, of what the window accomplished, what completed, what is in progress, and what is next.
- **Current with the board.**
  The summary matches the board's Status.
- **The board they asked for.**
  The summary covers the board they name, every board, or the one initiative they name.
- **A paragraph for management.**
  The user has one paragraph on what the window delivered for the initiatives it serves.

## Prerequisites

Read these files first.

- [Standalone Body](standalone-body.md)
- [Board Queue](board-queue.md)

## Operations

### *Populate* Hot-fix Body

One hot-fix body from a confirmed defect.

**Inputs:** Hot-fix number, confirmed target, problem, design, criteria, theme label and output path.

- Populate the body from the standalone [Template](standalone-body.md#template) at the supplied output path.
  - The work must meet [Definition](#definition).
  - The title must meet the shared [Titles](issue-body.md#titles) conditions and the hot-fix [Titles](#titles).
  - The Overview must name the confirmed target as [Target](#target) states.
  - The Problem and Proposal must meet [Problem and Proposal](issue-body.md#problem-and-proposal).
  - All populated fields must meet [Fields](#fields).

## Fields

### Definition

- A hot-fix fixes a defect in one long-lived branch outside the initiative, epic and task branch structure, as that branch stands, such as `main` or `workspace`. That branch is its target.
- Work that needs an open initiative, epic or task is not a hot-fix.

### Target

- The Overview names the target in one line of its own, `Target:` and the branch in a code span: ``Target: `workspace` ``.
- The target is a long-lived branch its project declares, as [Branches](delivery-branches.md#branches) states, confirmed with the hot-fix's placement.

### Titles

- The title is `[F00] Name: Subtitle`. The `[F00]` prefix is what makes an issue a hot-fix.
- The labels are `type:hot-fix`, the `theme:*` label of the board it sits on, and the [priority label](board-queue.md#priority-sets) for priority 10.
- `F` is the hot-fix number. Hot-fixes count from `00`.

### Membership

- A hot-fix belongs to no initiative or epic, and names no Depends on or Joins.
- It sits on its theme's board.
- Its priority 10, which its [Titles](#titles) label carries, ranks it nowhere: the queue places it by its [Board Status](hotfix.md#board-status), outside the priority sets.

### Debt

- A hot-fix fixes the debt its delivery finds as a unit's [Debt](delivery-plan.md#debt) states.

### Sections

- A hot-fix has the [standalone body](standalone-body.md)'s sections.

# Hot-fix

A hot-fix's board status, delivery unit and branch, delivering pull requests, hold and delivery record.

## Prerequisites

Read these files first.

- [Hot-fix Body](hotfix-body.md)
- [Issue](issue.md)
- [Board](board.md)
- [Board Delivery](board-delivery.md)
- [Placement](placement.md)
- [Repository Labels](repository-labels.md)
- [Agent Review](agent-review.md)

## Operations

### *Open* Hot-fix Issue

A source issue's hot-fix number and labels, ready for its body rewrite.

**Inputs:** Repository and source issue identity.

1. Run [Select Tracker Number](issue.md#select-tracker-number) with the hot-fix prefix letter.
2. Run [Ensure Repository Labels](repository-labels.md#ensure-repository-labels) with the labels hot-fix [Titles](hotfix-body.md#titles) name.
3. Return the hot-fix number to the caller, which rewrites and saves the issue's body, title and labels, then places it through [Settle Hot-fix Board Status](#settle-hot-fix-board-status), as its [placement](placement.md#disposition-conditions) orders.

### *Hold* Hot-fix Unit

One confirmed hot-fix unit held for its session.

**Inputs:** Hot-fix issue, board identity, the board items the caller last read, field definitions, output directory and assignee login.

1. Run [Record Dispatch Status](board-delivery.md#record-dispatch-status) with the hot-fix issue for In Progress and the supplied board evidence. That status is the hold [Delivery Unit](#delivery-unit) defines.
2. Return the confirmed status, or the discrepancy, to the caller. The session starts only once it is confirmed.

### *Release* Hot-fix Hold

A held hot-fix returned to the work the delivery plan offers.

**Inputs:** Board identity and the held hot-fix's issue identity.

1. Run [Capture Issue Development](issue.md#capture-issue-development) for the hot-fix issue.
   - Refuse the release while its [Delivery Unit](#delivery-unit) is running or unrecorded, and return the pull request that makes it so to the caller.
2. Run [Place Issue on Board](board.md#place-issue-on-board) with the supplied board, the hot-fix issue and Ready.
3. Return the saved item and its Status to the caller.

### *Record* Hot-fix Delivery

One hot-fix body with its confirmed delivery and verified criteria recorded.

**Inputs:** Hot-fix JSON, pull request records, complete issue-link snapshot, delivering pull request number, verified criterion ids and output body file.

1. Run [Sync Hot-fix Issue](#sync-hot-fix-issue) with the hot-fix JSON, records as `--prs`, snapshot as `--links`, delivery number as `--pr`, verified ids as `--tick` and output as `--fix`. Tick only criteria the caller has verified.
2. Return the body and eligibility findings; the caller publishes the body and closes the tracker issue, as [Delivery Record](#delivery-record) states.

### *Settle* Hot-fix Board Status

One hot-fix's board item set where [Board Status](#board-status) places it.

**Inputs:** Board identity and the hot-fix issue identity.

1. Run [Read Tracker Issue](issue.md#read-tracker-issue) for the hot-fix's current state.
2. Run [Read Board State](board.md#read-board-state) for its item and Status. A hot-fix with no item has no Status.
3. Apply the status [Board Status](#board-status) gives that state and Status:
   - **A status.**
     - Run [Place Issue on Board](board.md#place-issue-on-board) with the supplied board, the hot-fix issue and that status, which adds the item where the board has none.
   - **Off the board, with an item.**
     - Run [Remove Board Item](board.md#remove-board-item) with the supplied board owner and number and the item id Read Board State returned.
   - **Off the board, with no item.**
     - Change nothing; the hot-fix already stands off the board.
4. Return the settled item, its removal, or the unchanged board to the caller.

## Fields

### Board Status

- An open hot-fix stands In Review while a [delivering pull request](#delivering-pull-request) of it is open and ready for review, and In Progress while one is an open draft.
- Otherwise an open hot-fix is Ready, whatever any initiative's or epic's priority, and In Progress once it holds In Progress or In Review. It reaches the board as its [placement](placement.md#disposition-conditions) orders.
- A closed hot-fix takes the status [Status Changes](board-delivery.md#status-changes) gives a closed issue.
- No initiative or epic waits on a hot-fix, and a hot-fix waits on none.

### Delivery Unit

- An open hot-fix Ready on the board is a delivery unit of its own, whatever any epic's state. Its issue is the unit's task issue; it has no row and no epic record.
- Its Coverage is every criterion it carries. Its record folder takes its prefix and title name as a task id and Description.
- Its component lies on its [target](hotfix-body.md#target), which its session's work item declares.
- **Running.**
  Any open pull request whose Development field links it, draft or not, makes it running: it is neither offered nor released, and an In Progress status it holds stays its hold. A linking pull request is enough to keep a second session off it, while only a [delivering pull request](#delivering-pull-request) is merged or recorded as its fix.
- **Unrecorded.**
  A merged delivering pull request on an open hot-fix leaves its merge awaiting the [delivery record](#delivery-record), whoever merged it.
- **Hold.**
  Its In Progress status is its hold: a dispatch sets it, and a return to Ready releases it while it is neither running nor unrecorded.

### Branch

A hot-fix's branch is cut from its [target](hotfix-body.md#target), which its `unit` line names as its base, and is named for its prefix in lowercase and hyphenated with a slug of at most four words from its title's name: `f00-key-validation`. Its worktree is named by its branch, as a task branch's is.

### Delivering Pull Request

- A pull request delivers a hot-fix when its title opens with the hot-fix's prefix, `[F00] Purpose`, it lives in the hot-fix's repository, its base is the hot-fix's [target](hotfix-body.md#target), and its Development field links the hot-fix.
- It is opened from the hot-fix's [branch](#branch), as a draft.
- It is marked ready for review only once its review cycle is complete: its current [agent review](agent-review.md#review-record) leaves every finding fixed.
- A reopened hot-fix still counts a delivering pull request merged before it reopened, since the issue records no reopen time.
- A pull request into a branch the body named as its target before an edit stops counting, since the body names the current target.

### Delivery Record

- A hot-fix's merge is recorded on its own issue alone: its criteria and delivering pull request, then its closure. It records nothing on an epic or initiative.
- Its board item follows [Board Status](#board-status) once the issue closes.

## Commands

### Sync Hot-fix Issue

Records the pull request that delivers a hot-fix, open or merged, ticks verified criteria, and reports whether it is closable.

**Inputs:** Hot-fix JSON, pull request records, complete issue-link snapshot, delivering pull request number, verified criterion ids and output file.

- A `--pr` that does not deliver the hot-fix is refused, naming the condition it fails.
- `<criterion-ids>` is a comma-separated list of verified criterion ids.

```bash
cd "<workspace>" && "<workspace>/scripts/sbx" python3 skills/work-planner/scripts/sync.py '<hot-fix-json-file>' --prs '<pull-request-records-file>' --links '<issue-link-snapshot-file>' --pr '<pull-request-number>' --tick '<criterion-ids>' --fix '<output-body-file>'
```

**Example:**

```bash
cd "<workspace>" && "<workspace>/scripts/sbx" python3 skills/work-planner/scripts/sync.py issue-874.json --prs prs.json --links links.json --pr 950 --tick AC1 --fix fixed-874.md
```

# Standup Report

A board progress report for a selected window, formatted for pasting into Slack.

## Prerequisites

Read these files first.

- When no window start is supplied, read [Standup Configuration](../configuration.md#standup).
- [Hot-fix Body](hotfix-body.md)
- [Hot-fix](hotfix.md)

## Operations

### *Compose* Standup Report

The copyable report and any missing-evidence findings.

**Inputs:** Board items, pull request records, complete issue-link snapshot, optional window start, initiative filter, resolved off-board initiative records and output paths.

1. Require the complete issue-link snapshot.
2. Run [Summarise Progress](#summarise-progress), passing items as `--items`, pull requests as `--prs`, links as `--links`, the selected start as `--since`, the filter as `--initiative` and every resolved initiative as `--initiatives`.
3. If initiative references remain unresolved, return them for the caller to supply.
4. Write the management paragraph from the rendered Initiatives and Completed sections.
   - It must meet [Management Paragraph](#management-paragraph).
5. Run [Summarise Progress](#summarise-progress) with the same inputs and the paragraph file as `--summary`.
6. Return the report and separate unresolved findings.
   - The report must meet [Fields](#fields).

## Fields

### Scope

When no start date is supplied, the window follows [Standup Configuration](../configuration.md#standup). A supplied start date selects another window, such as the previous working day for a daily standup. An initiative filter names one initiative, qualified by repository when its number is ambiguous.

Each repository numbers its own initiatives, and an initiative's epics and task issues may live in other repositories. Each item's place follows the Work Breakdown links, or for a task issue the pull request whose Development field links it. A pull request counts towards the epic of its reference in the epic's repository or its initiative's.

### Sections

The management paragraph is set off by blank lines, with the board's link beneath the heading.

- **Initiatives.**
  One line for each initiative with work under Completed or In progress, its title's name and subtitle, opening with the mark of its state. One off the board is done when closed, else in progress. An item works for the initiative whose table links its epic and for the one its epic's title names.
- **Completed.**
  Items Done whose issue closed in the window, grouped under their epic, and tasks whose pull requests merged in it. Closing is when an issue became Done; an issue the board caught up with later still falls on its closing date.
- **In progress.**
  Epics In Progress or In Review and task issues In Progress, each epic with its open pull requests, or else its next task.
- **Next.**
  The five Ready items, each epic with its next task, and a count of the rest.
  - Ready hot-fixes lead.
  - They rank by the priority label of the initiative their epic belongs to, then by their epic's own.
  - An epic is placed ahead of any listed epic naming it, so a supplier reads before the work drawing on it. An epic names another when a task row names one of its rows or the initiative row names it whole.
- **Hot-fixes.**
  Each [hot-fix](hotfix-body.md) follows the epic groups of Completed, In progress or Next as its status places it, with its [delivering pull requests](hotfix.md#delivering-pull-request) beneath. An initiative filter leaves hot-fixes out.
- **Key.**
  I Initiative, E Epic, W Work Item and F Hot-fix. Opening marks are ✅ done, 🔄 in progress (an initiative, epic or hot-fix open and not In Review, or a task issue In Progress), 👀 in review (an initiative, epic or hot-fix In Review, or a pull request ready for review), 📝 draft and ▶️ ready.

### Management Paragraph

One plain-language paragraph describes what the window delivered as outcomes for the initiatives it serves, grounded in Initiatives and Completed. It carries no references, links, task ids or tool names, and leaves out work in progress and next. With nothing completed, it says so in one sentence.

### Unresolved Evidence

An unresolved initiative identifies its number and repository for the caller to fetch. An off-board dependency is blocked. An epic with unreadable Work Breakdown is summarised without tasks and returned as a finding. Unresolved lines are separate from the copyable report.

# Standup Report

A board progress report for a selected window, formatted for pasting into Slack.

## Prerequisites

Read these files first.

- When no window start is supplied, read [Standup Configuration](../configuration.md#standup).
- [Hot-fix Body](hotfix-body.md)
- [Hot-fix](hotfix.md)

## Operations

### *Compose* Standup Report

The copyable report and any missing-evidence findings.

**Inputs:** Board items, pull request records, complete issue-link snapshot, optional window start, initiative filter, resolved off-board initiative records and output paths.

1. Require the complete issue-link snapshot.
2. Run [Summarise Progress](#summarise-progress), passing items as `--items`, pull requests as `--prs`, links as `--links`, the selected start as `--since`, the filter as `--initiative` and every resolved initiative as `--initiatives`.
3. If initiative references remain unresolved, return them for the caller to supply.
4. Write the management paragraph from the rendered Initiatives and Completed sections.
   - It must meet [Management Paragraph](#management-paragraph).
5. Run [Summarise Progress](#summarise-progress) with the same inputs and the paragraph file as `--summary`.
6. Return the report and separate unresolved findings.
   - The report must meet [Fields](#fields).

## Fields

### Scope

When no window start is supplied, the window uses the default in [Standup Configuration](../configuration.md#standup). A supplied start date selects another window, such as the previous working day for a daily standup. An initiative filter names one initiative, qualified by repository when its number is ambiguous.

Each repository numbers its own initiatives, and an initiative's epics and task issues may live in other repositories. Each item's place follows the Work Breakdown links, or for a task issue the pull request whose Development field links it. A pull request counts towards the epic of its reference in the epic's repository or its initiative's.

### Sections

The management paragraph is set off by blank lines, with the board's link beneath the heading.

- **Initiatives.**
  One line for each initiative with work under Completed or In progress, its title's name and subtitle, opening with the mark of its state. One off the board is done when closed, else in progress. An item works for the initiative whose table links its epic and for the one its epic's title names.
- **Completed.**
  Items Done whose issue closed in the window, grouped under their epic, and tasks whose pull requests merged in it. Closing is when an issue became Done; an issue the board caught up with later still falls on its closing date.
- **In progress.**
  Epics In Progress or In Review and task issues In Progress, each epic with its open pull requests, or else its next task.
- **Next.**
  The five Ready items, each epic with its next task, and a count of the rest.
  - Ready hot-fixes lead.
  - They rank by the priority label of the initiative their epic belongs to, then by their epic's own.
  - An epic is placed ahead of any listed epic naming it, so a supplier reads before the work drawing on it. An epic names another when a task row names one of its rows or the initiative row names it whole.
- **Hot-fixes.**
  Each [hot-fix](hotfix-body.md) follows the epic groups of Completed, In progress or Next as its status places it, with its [delivering pull requests](hotfix.md#delivering-pull-request) beneath. An initiative filter leaves hot-fixes out.
- **Key.**
  I Initiative, E Epic, W Work Item and F Hot-fix. Opening marks are ✅ done, 🔄 in progress (an initiative, epic or hot-fix open and not In Review, or a task issue In Progress), 👀 in review (an initiative, epic or hot-fix In Review, or a pull request ready for review), 📝 draft and ▶️ ready.

One plain-language paragraph describes what the window delivered as outcomes for the initiatives it serves, grounded in Initiatives and Completed. It carries no references, links, task ids or tool names, and leaves out work in progress and next. With nothing completed, it says so in one sentence.

An unresolved initiative identifies its number and repository for the caller to fetch. An off-board dependency is blocked. An epic with unreadable Work Breakdown is summarised without tasks and returned as a finding. Unresolved lines are separate from the copyable report.
